verses.12:45: Moreover, looking to the most excellent reward laid up for those who fall asleep in godliness, it was a holy and pious thought. Therefore he made atonement for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin.
verses.13:1: In the one hundred and forty-ninth year, word reached those with Judas that Antiochus Eupator was coming with multitudes against Judea,
verses.13:2: and with him Lysias his guardian, who was in charge of the affairs of state, each having a Greek force of one hundred and ten thousand foot soldiers, and five thousand three hundred horsemen, and twenty-two elephants, and three hundred chariots armed with scythes.
verses.13:3: Menelaus also joined them, and with great hypocrisy urged Antiochus on, not for the safety of his country, but supposing that he would be established in his office.
verses.13:4: But the King of kings stirred up the wrath of Antiochus against the wicked wretch; and when Lysias pointed out that this man was the cause of all the evils, the king commanded that they take him to Berea and put him to death there, as is the custom in that place.
verses.13:5: Now there is in that place a tower fifty cubits high, full of ashes, and it had a circular contrivance sloping steeply on every side down into the ashes.
verses.13:6: There all thrust down to destruction anyone guilty of sacrilege, or anyone who has achieved preeminence in any other evils.
verses.13:7: By such a fate it came to pass that the transgressor Menelaus died, without even obtaining burial in the earth;
verses.13:8: and most justly so; for since he had committed many sins against the altar, whose fire and ashes were holy, in ashes he received his death.
verses.13:9: Now the king came on, hardened in his thoughts, intending to inflict upon the Jews things worse than those that had been done in the time of his father.
verses.13:10: When Judas learned of this, he commanded the multitude to call upon the Lord day and night, that if ever at any other time, so now He would come to the aid of those who were about to be deprived of the law, their country, and the holy temple,
verses.13:11: and that He would not permit the people, who had only just begun to revive a little, to fall into the hands of the blasphemous nations.
verses.13:12: When all had done this together, and had implored the merciful Lord with weeping and fasting and lying prostrate for three days without ceasing, Judas encouraged them and commanded them to stand ready.
verses.13:13: And taking counsel privately with the elders, he resolved that before the king's army should invade Judea and gain control of the city, they would march out and decide the matter with the help of God.
verses.13:14: Committing the outcome to the Lord of the world, he exhorted those who were with him to contend nobly even to death for the laws, the temple, the city, their country, and their way of life; and he pitched his camp near Modein.
verses.13:15: Having given to those with him the watchword, "Victory of God," he attacked the royal pavilion by night with the finest chosen young men, slew about two thousand men in the camp, and brought down the foremost of the elephants together with the one in its tower;
verses.13:16: and in the end they filled the camp with terror and confusion, and withdrew in triumph.
verses.13:17: This had been accomplished just as the day was beginning to dawn, through the protecting care of the Lord that aided him.
verses.13:18: Now the king, having had a taste of the boldness of the Jews, tried to take those places by stratagem.
verses.13:19: He marched against Beth-zur, a small fortress of the Jews; he advanced, he was driven back, he met with reverses, he was defeated.
verses.13:20: And Judas sent in the necessary supplies to those who were within.
verses.13:21: But Rhodocus, from the Jewish ranks, disclosed the secrets to the enemy; he was sought out, arrested, and imprisoned.
verses.13:22: The king negotiated a second time with those in Beth-zur, gave his right hand in pledge, received theirs, departed, attacked those with Judas, was worsted,
verses.13:23: heard that Philip, who had been left in charge of the affairs of state, had lost his senses in Antioch, was dismayed, appealed to the Jews, yielded, and swore to all just terms, came to a settlement and offered sacrifice, honored the sanctuary and the place, showed kindness,
verses.13:24: and welcomed Maccabeus, left Hegemonides as governor from Ptolemais to the Gennerites,
verses.13:25: and came to Ptolemais. The people of Ptolemais were displeased with the treaty, for they were exceedingly fearful; they wished to annul the stipulations.
verses.13:26: Lysias stepped up to the tribunal, made the best defense possible, persuaded and pacified them, made them well disposed, and departed to Antioch. Thus went the expedition of the king and his return.
verses.14:1: Now after a period of three years, word reached Judas and his men that Demetrius the son of Seleucus, having sailed in through the harbor of Tripolis with a mighty host and a fleet,
verses.14:2: had seized control of the land, having put to death Antiochus and his guardian Lysias.
verses.14:3: Now a certain Alcimus, who had formerly been high priest, but had willfully defiled himself in the times of separation, realizing that in no way whatever was there any safety for him, nor any further access to the holy altar,
verses.14:4: came to King Demetrius about the one hundred and fifty-first year, presenting to him a crown of gold and a palm branch, and besides these, some of the customary boughs of the temple. And on that day he kept silent.
verses.14:5: But when he found an opportunity favorable to his own folly, being summoned into council by Demetrius and asked in what disposition and counsel the Jews stood, he answered to these things:
verses.14:6: "Those among the Jews who are called Hasideans, whose leader is Judas Maccabeus, keep up war and stir up sedition, not allowing the kingdom to attain stability.
verses.14:7: Therefore, being deprived of my ancestral glory—meaning the high priesthood—I have now come a second time,
verses.14:8: first, genuinely caring for the interests pertaining to the king, and second, having regard also for my own fellow citizens; for by the recklessness of the men just mentioned, our entire nation suffers no small misfortune.
verses.14:9: Now having learned each of these matters, O king, take thought both for the country and for our hard-pressed nation, according to the gracious kindness which you hold toward all.
verses.14:10: For as long as Judas remains alive, it is impossible for affairs of state to attain peace."
verses.14:11: When such words had been spoken by him, the rest of the Friends, who were hostile toward Judas, swiftly inflamed Demetrius still further.
verses.14:12: Immediately he chose Nicanor, who had been master of the elephants, and having appointed him governor of Judea, he sent him forth,
verses.14:13: giving him written instructions to put Judas himself to death, to scatter those who were with him, and to establish Alcimus as high priest of the greatest temple.
verses.14:14: And the Gentiles throughout Judea who had fled from Judas flocked in droves to join Nicanor, supposing that the misfortunes and calamities of the Jews would turn to their own prosperity.
verses.14:15: Now when they heard of the advance of Nicanor and the assault of the Gentiles, they sprinkled earth upon themselves and implored Him who established His people forever, and who always with a manifestation upholds His own portion.
verses.14:16: And when the leader gave the command, he immediately marched out from there and engaged them at the village of Lessau.
verses.14:17: Now Simon, the brother of Judas, had encountered Nicanor, yet had slowly suffered a setback because of the sudden consternation caused by the adversaries.
verses.14:18: Nevertheless, Nicanor, hearing of the valor which Judas and his men possessed, and their courage in the struggles for their homeland, shrank from bringing the decision to the issue of bloodshed.
verses.14:19: Therefore he sent Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to give and to receive pledges of peace.
verses.14:20: After thorough consideration had been given to these matters, and the leader had laid them before the multitudes, and a unanimous consent appeared, they agreed to the treaty.
verses.14:21: They appointed a day on which they would meet together in private; a litter came forward from each side, and they set down seats.
verses.14:22: Judas stationed armed men in readiness at the strategic places, lest any treachery should suddenly arise from the enemy; and they held a fitting conference.
verses.14:23: Nicanor remained in Jerusalem and did nothing amiss, and he dismissed the thronging crowds that had gathered together.
verses.14:24: He kept Judas continually in his presence, for he had become deeply attached to the man in his heart.
verses.14:25: He urged him to marry and raise children; so he married, settled down in quietness, and shared in the common life.
verses.14:26: Now Alcimus, perceiving their goodwill toward one another, took the treaty that had been made and came to Demetrius, and told him that Nicanor was disloyal to the affairs of state, for he had appointed Judas, the conspirator against his kingdom, to be his successor.
verses.14:27: Then the king became furious, and provoked by the slanders of that utterly wicked man, he wrote to Nicanor, declaring that he was deeply displeased with the treaty, and commanding him to send Maccabeus as a prisoner to Antioch without delay.
verses.14:28: When these words reached Nicanor, he was greatly troubled and took it hard that he should set aside what had been agreed upon, seeing that the man had done no wrong.
verses.14:29: Yet since it was not possible to oppose the king, he watched for a favorable opportunity to carry out the order by stratagem.
verses.14:30: But Maccabeus, seeing that Nicanor was conducting himself more harshly toward him, and had grown more abrupt in his accustomed greeting, realized that this harshness did not come from good intent; so he gathered together not a few of his men and concealed himself from Nicanor.
verses.14:31: When the other realized that he had been shrewdly outmaneuvered by the man, he came to the greatest and holy temple while the priests were offering the appointed sacrifices, and commanded them to hand over the man.
verses.14:32: And when they declared with oaths that they did not know where the man he sought might be,
verses.14:33: stretching out his right hand toward the sanctuary, he swore these words: "Unless you deliver Judas to me as a prisoner, I will level this sacred precinct of God to a plain, and I will tear down the altar, and I will raise up here a splendid temple to Dionysus."
verses.14:34: Having spoken these words, he departed. Then the priests, stretching out their hands toward heaven, called upon Him who is ever the Defender of our nation, saying:
verses.14:35: "You, O Lord, who are in need of nothing at all, were well pleased that a temple of Your dwelling should be among us.
verses.14:36: And now, O holy Lord of all sanctification, preserve forever undefiled this house that has been so recently cleansed."
verses.14:37: Now a certain Razis, one of the elders of Jerusalem, was denounced to Nicanor—a man who loved his fellow citizens, was very well spoken of, and because of his goodwill was called Father of the Jews.
verses.14:38: For in the former times of separation he had been brought under charges for Judaism, and with all earnestness had risked both body and soul for Judaism.
verses.14:39: Now Nicanor, wishing to make manifest the hostility which he held toward the Jews, sent more than five hundred soldiers to seize him.
verses.14:40: For he thought that by seizing him he would bring calamity upon them.
verses.14:41: When the troops were about to capture the tower, and were forcing the courtyard door and giving orders to bring fire and set the doors ablaze, finding himself surrounded on every side, he fell upon his sword,
verses.14:42: choosing to die nobly rather than fall into the hands of wicked men and suffer outrages unworthy of his own noble birth.
verses.14:43: But because he missed his mark with the stroke in the haste of the struggle, and the crowds were rushing inside through the doorways, he ran bravely up onto the wall and cast himself down courageously among the crowds.
verses.14:44: As they swiftly drew back and an interval opened up, he fell right in the middle of the empty space.
verses.14:45: Yet still breathing and inflamed with fierce passion, he rose up while his blood gushed forth like a fountain; and though his wounds were grievous, he ran through the midst of the crowds and stood upon a steep rock,
verses.14:46: and now completely drained of blood, he tore out his entrails, and taking them in both hands, hurled them upon the crowds; and calling upon Him who is Sovereign over life and spirit to restore these very things to him again, in this manner he died.
verses.15:1: Now Nicanor, having learned that Judas and those with him were in the regions of Samaria, resolved to fall upon them with all safety on the day of rest.
verses.15:2: And the Jews who followed him under compulsion said, "By no means destroy them so savagely and barbarously, but give honor to the day that has been preeminently honored with holiness by Him who beholds all things."
verses.15:3: Then that thrice-accursed man asked whether there is a Sovereign in heaven who has commanded to observe the Sabbath day.
verses.15:4: And they declared, "There is the living Lord Himself, the Sovereign in heaven, who has commanded the seventh day to be observed."
verses.15:5: And the other said, "I also am a sovereign on the earth, who commands that arms be taken up and the king's business be fulfilled." Yet he did not succeed in accomplishing his ruthless design.
verses.15:6: Now Nicanor, bearing himself loftily with all assurance, had determined to establish a common course for Judas and those with him.
verses.15:7: But Maccabeus trusted continually, with all hope, that he would obtain help from the Lord.
verses.15:8: And he exhorted those with him not to fear the onslaught of the Gentiles, but keeping in mind the former acts of help that had come to them from heaven, to expect even now the victory that would come to them from the Almighty.
verses.15:9: And encouraging them from the Law and the Prophets, and reminding them also of the struggles they had already accomplished, he made them more eager.
verses.15:10: And having aroused their spirits, he gave his orders, at the same time pointing out the treachery of the Gentiles and their breaking of oaths.
verses.15:11: Thus arming each of them, not so much with the security of shields and spears as with the encouragement of good words, and relating besides a trustworthy dream, he gladdened them all exceedingly.
verses.15:12: Now the vision of it was this: Onias, who had been high priest, a noble and good man, modest in his bearing, gentle in his disposition, speaking fittingly, and trained from childhood in all things belonging to virtue—this man was stretching out his hands and praying for the whole community of the Jews.
verses.15:13: Then in the same manner there appeared a man distinguished by gray hair and glory, and a wondrous and most majestic preeminence was about him.
verses.15:14: And Onias answered and said, "This is a lover of the brethren, who prays much for the people and the holy city—Jeremiah, the prophet of God."
verses.15:15: Then Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and delivered to Judas a golden sword, and as he gave it, he addressed him thus:
verses.15:16: "Take the holy sword, a gift from God, through which you shall crush the adversaries."
verses.15:17: Now being encouraged by the words of Judas, which were exceedingly noble and able to incite to valor and make manly the souls of young men, they resolved not to carry on a campaign, but to charge nobly, and engaging hand to hand with all courage, to decide the issue, because the city, the holy things, and the temple were in danger.
verses.15:18: For their fear for wives and children, and also for brethren and kinsmen, was of lesser account to them, while their greatest and foremost fear was for the consecrated sanctuary.
verses.15:19: And those who were shut up in the city also had no slight anguish, being troubled over the battle in the open field.
verses.15:20: Now when all were already awaiting the coming decision, and the enemies had already drawn near, and the army was drawn up in battle array, and the beasts were stationed in a favorable position, and the cavalry was arrayed on the flanks,
verses.15:21: Maccabeus, beholding the presence of the multitudes, the varied array of weapons, and the fierceness of the beasts in their favorable position, stretched out his hands toward heaven and called upon the Lord who works wonders, knowing that it is not through weapons, but according as He decides, that He secures victory for those who are worthy.
verses.15:22: And calling upon Him, he spoke after this manner: "You, O Master, sent Your angel in the days of Hezekiah king of Judea, and he slew from the camp of Sennacherib as many as one hundred and eighty-five thousand.
verses.15:23: And now, O Sovereign of the heavens, send a good angel before us to bring dread and trembling;
verses.15:24: by the greatness of Your arm let those who come with blasphemy against Your holy people be struck with terror." And with these words he ended.
verses.15:25: Now Nicanor and those with him advanced with trumpets and battle songs,
verses.15:26: while Judas and those with him met the enemies in battle with invocation and prayers.
verses.15:27: And fighting with their hands while praying to God in their hearts, they struck down no fewer than thirty-five thousand, rejoicing greatly in the care of God.
verses.15:28: And when the engagement was over and they were returning with joy, they recognized Nicanor lying fallen in his full armor.
verses.15:29: Then a shout and commotion arose, and they blessed the Sovereign in the language of their fathers.
verses.15:30: And he who in every way, in body and soul, was the foremost champion for his fellow citizens, and who had preserved the goodwill of his youth toward his countrymen, commanded that they cut off the head of Nicanor, and his hand with the shoulder, and bear them to Jerusalem.
verses.15:31: And when he arrived there, having called together his countrymen and stationed the priests before the altar, he sent for those from the citadel.
verses.15:32: And having displayed the head of the vile Nicanor and the hand of the blasphemer, which he had stretched out against the holy house of the Almighty with arrogant boasting,
verses.15:33: and having cut out the tongue of the ungodly Nicanor, he declared that it should be piecemeal for the birds, and commanded the wages of his folly to be hung up opposite the temple.
verses.15:34: And they all offered blessing toward heaven to the manifest Lord, saying, "Blessed be He who has kept His own place undefiled!"
verses.15:35: And he hung the head of Nicanor from the citadel, visible to all and a clear sign of the help of the Lord.
verses.15:36: And they all decreed by a common resolution by no means to leave this day unmarked, but to keep as a notable day the thirteenth day of the twelfth month—called Adar in the Lord's language—one day before the day of Mordecai.
verses.15:37: Therefore, since the affairs concerning Nicanor turned out in this way, and since from those times the city has been held by the Hebrews, I myself also will here bring this narrative to an end.
verses.15:38: And if it has been well and aptly composed, that is what I myself desired; but if plainly and mediocrely, that was all I was able to attain.
verses.15:39: Just as drinking wine by itself, and likewise water by itself again, is harmful, whereas wine mixed with water at once produces a delightful charm, so also the skillful arrangement of the discourse delights the ears of those who read the composition. And here shall be the end.

notes.1:8: The Greek text reads "brought forth" (exegagomen) rather than "lighted" or "kindled" (exepsamen) found in some manuscripts.
notes.1:10: The Greek text reads "eighty-eighth" (without "one hundred"), whereas other manuscripts read "one hundred and eighty-eighth" (Seleucid era, 124 BC); it also places a period after "in Jerusalem" rather than opening the salutation with "Those in Jerusalem."
notes.1:21: The Greek text shifts unexpectedly to the first-person plural ("reported to us"), reflecting the style of the underlying letter.
notes.1:35: The Greek text omits the verb "favored" (echarizeto) found in some manuscripts after the relative pronoun, creating an elliptical clause rendered here as referring to the revenues of the sacred enclosure.
notes.1:36: The Greek text reads "Nephthar" in both places, whereas some manuscripts read "Nephthai" (akin to "naphtha") in the second occurrence.
notes.2:14: The Greek text reads "these things" (tauta) rather than "all things" (panta) found in some manuscripts.
notes.2:28: The Greek text reads "lacking strength" (atonountes), whereas other manuscripts read "taking pains" (diaponountes).
notes.2:29: The Greek text reads "to renovate" (enkainizein), whereas other witnesses read "to do encaustic painting" (enkaiein).
notes.3:6: The Greek text reads prosenegkein ("apply" or "contribute") rather than prosekein ("pertain") found in some other witnesses.
notes.3:11: The clause "not as the impious Simon had falsely accused" renders a compressed Greek construction (ouch houtos diaballon) preserved in this text.
notes.3:18: Following the Greek text here (which includes the negative particle me, as in Codex Alexandrinus), the clause expresses purpose ("that the place might not be about to come into contempt") rather than cause.
notes.3:26: "Most fair in speech" translates the Greek glossan ("tongue/speech," as in Codex Alexandrinus), where other manuscripts read doxan ("glory" or "splendor").
notes.3:28: The Greek singular participle epegnokota refers to Heliodorus himself acknowledging the sovereign power, whereas some manuscripts use a plural participle referring to his attendants and add "of God."
notes.4:4: The Greek source reads "Coele-Phoenicia and Syria" (Koiles Phoinikes kai Syrias) rather than the more common "Coele-Syria and Phoenicia," and is rendered literally here.
notes.4:12: The Greek source reads "those in our time" (ton eph' hemon) rather than the variant "the youths" (ton ephebon). "Under the Greek hat" renders hypo petason, referring to the broad-brimmed hat worn by Greek gymnasium youths.
notes.4:19: The Greek source specifies three hundred drachmas of silver and moves directly into verse 20 without the longer transitional clause found in some manuscripts regarding the impropriety of sacrifice and the sender's intent.
notes.4:33: The Greek source reads apenegken ("reported" or "brought charges") rather than the textual variant apelegchen ("exposed" or "rebuked").
notes.4:40: The Greek text names the leader Auranus (some witnesses read Tyrannus) and describes him as advanced in "ignorance" (agnoian) rather than the variant "folly" (anoian).
notes.5:3: The Greek text reads kamaton ("toils" or "exertions"), whereas some manuscripts and editions read kamakon ("spear-shafts" or "pikes").
notes.5:10: The Greek text reads patroou nomou ("ancestral law"), whereas other manuscripts read patroou taphou ("ancestral tomb").
notes.5:24: Greek mysarches ("commander of the Mysians") refers to an officer leading Mysian mercenary troops in the Seleucid army.
notes.5:26: The Greek text reads katestesen ("put down" or "subdued"), whereas other witnesses read katestrosen ("struck down") or katesphaxen ("slaughtered").
notes.6:2: Greek Dios xeniou denotes Zeus Xenius ("Friend" or "Protector of Strangers"). The Greek text reads kathos etynchanon ("just as they were"), referring to the character of the inhabitants, whereas some witnesses read enetynchanon ("as they petitioned").
notes.6:19: Greek tympanon refers to a drum-shaped wooden rack or frame on which victims were stretched and beaten.
notes.6:23: The Greek text reads politeias ("way of life" or "citizenship"), whereas other manuscripts read polias ("gray hair").
notes.6:29: The Greek text concisely omits the participle metabalonton ("turning") found in some witnesses, though the double accusative clearly conveys that his escort turned their earlier goodwill into hostility.
notes.7:11: The Greek text reads kekletai ("have been called", as in Codex Alexandrinus) rather than kektēmai ("I possess" or "I received").
notes.7:18: The Greek text reads mallon ("any further" or "rather", as in Codex Alexandrinus) rather than matēn ("in vain").
notes.7:21: The Greek text reads tōn anthrōpōn ("of the men", as in Codex Alexandrinus) rather than autōn ("of them").
notes.7:36: The Greek text reads peptōkasin ("have fallen [under]"), referring to coming under God's covenant of everlasting life; some manuscripts read pepōkasin ("have drunk of").
notes.7:37: The Greek text reads tychēn ("fortune" or "lot", as in Codex Alexandrinus) rather than psychēn ("soul" or "life"), and uses the plural participle epikaloumenoi ("as we call upon"), uniting the youngest brother with his brothers.
notes.8:16: The Greek source text reads "by the captives" (tois desmiois), whereas other manuscripts read "by the enemies" (tois polemiois).
notes.8:20: The Greek source text names eight thousand entering the battle and then refers to "the six thousand" who defeated the one hundred and twenty thousand; other witnesses read "the eight thousand" in both places.
notes.8:23: With the nominative participle paranagnous, the Greek source text presents Judas himself as reading the sacred book, whereas other witnesses use an infinitive assigning the reading to Eleazar.
notes.8:25: The Greek source text reads "from the region, being constrained" here and "the observance (dike) before the Sabbath" in verse 26, where other manuscripts read "constrained by the hour" and "the hour before the Sabbath."
notes.9:8: The Greek source text reads antidokon without a following infinitive ("presumed to rival"), whereas other manuscripts read arti dokon ... epitassein ("who just now thought he could command").
notes.9:20: The Greek source text preserves a shorter greeting here, omitting the conditional "if" and the clause of thanksgiving to God found in other witnesses.
notes.10:4: The Greek text omits a verb after "with gentleness," so "dealt with" is supplied to complete the clause; other Greek manuscripts read "be disciplined" (paideuesthai).
notes.10:8: The Greek text reads "the tenth days" (tas dekatas hemeras), whereas other manuscripts read "these days" (tasde tas hemeras).
notes.10:10: The Greek text reads "the supreme Antiochus" (ton hypaton Antiochon) and "of the cities" (ton poleon), whereas other manuscripts read "Antiochus Eupator" (as in v. 13) and "of the wars" (ton polemon).
notes.10:14: The Greek text reads "against his own people" (pros tous idious), whereas other manuscripts read "against the Jews" (pros tous Ioudaious).
notes.10:33: The Greek text reads "forty days" here and "the twenty-fifth day" (without a number before "young men") in v. 35; other manuscripts read "four days" here and "the fifth day, twenty young men" in v. 35.
notes.11:5: Greek 'schoeni' (rendered 'leagues'), a measure of distance of roughly three to four miles each, matching Beth-zur's actual distance from Jerusalem; some manuscripts read 'stadia'.
notes.11:15: The Greek text here reads 'the secretary' (ho grammateus), whereas other manuscripts read 'the king' (ho basileus).
notes.11:21: Dioscorinthius (Greek Dios Korinthiou) is an otherwise unattested month name, possibly a textual corruption of the Macedonian month Dios or a local calendar month.
notes.11:23: The Greek text here reads 'who desired' (boulomenou) and 'the care of the Jews' (ton Ioudaion), whereas other manuscripts read 'we desiring' (boulomenoi) and 'their own affairs' (ton idion).
notes.11:31: Greek dapanemasin ('provisions' or 'expenditures'); other manuscripts read diaitemasin ('dietary customs' or 'way of life').
notes.12:13: The Greek word gephyroun literally means 'to bridge' or 'to lay a causeway'; some interpreters regard it as a textual variant for 'fortified with bridges' or an alternate designation alongside Caspin.
notes.12:20: This Greek text literally reads 'two thousand, and in addition seven thousand' horsemen, whereas other Septuagint manuscripts read 'two thousand five hundred.'
notes.12:45: The Greek reads eucharisterion (literally 'thank-offering' or 'gracious reward'), where other manuscripts read charisterion ('reward' or 'recompense').
notes.13:2: The Greek reads hekaston ('each'), indicating each leader having the Greek force; some commentators treat the pronoun as a textual crux.
notes.13:9: This Greek text reads bebaremenos ('hardened' or 'weighed down'), whereas other manuscripts read bebarbaromenos ('barbarous in spirit').
notes.13:15: The Greek synetheken ('brought down') is a variant of synekentesen ('pierced through'), and 'the one in its tower' literally translates 'the one in the house,' referring to the wooden howdah atop the elephant.
notes.13:19: This Greek text describes Beth-zur as 'a small fortress' (oligon), whereas other manuscripts read 'a strong fortress' (ochyron).
notes.13:24: This Greek text reads 'the Gennerites' (ton Genneron), where other Septuagint manuscripts read 'the Gerrenians' (ton Gerrenon).
notes.14:3: Greek amixias (also in 14:38) literally means 'non-intercourse' or 'separation,' referring to the period of estrangement and conflict when faithful Jews refused mingling with Gentiles.
notes.14:7: The Greek text here reads deuteron ('a second time'), whereas other Greek manuscripts read deuro ('here').
notes.14:16: The Greek text reads Lessaou ('Lessau'), whereas other manuscripts read Dessaou ('Dessau').
notes.14:17: The Greek text reads bradeos ('slowly'), whereas some manuscripts read bracheos ('slightly'); aphasian denotes sudden speechlessness or consternation.
notes.14:44: Greek keneona can mean either the 'empty space' opened by the retreating crowd or anatomically the 'flank' or 'abdomen' upon which Razis fell.
notes.15:6: The Greek text reads asphaleias ("assurance") and tropon ("way/course"), whereas other manuscripts read alazoneias ("arrogance") and tropaion ("public trophy/monument").
notes.15:17: The Greek text reads me strateuesthai ("not to carry on a campaign"), whereas other manuscripts read me stratopedeuesthai ("not to remain in camp").
notes.15:27: The Greek text reads epimeleia ("care"), whereas other manuscripts read epiphaneia ("manifestation" or "appearing").
notes.15:33: The Greek text compresses the first clause (without an explicit infinitive "to give") and uses epicheira ("wages," literally "hand-payment") as a play on Nicanor's severed hand.
notes.15:36: The Greek text reads te kyriake phone ("in the Lord's language"), a scribal variant for te Syriake phone ("in the Syrian/Aramaic language") found in other manuscripts.
